vignette:
Samuel is a twenty-year-old doctor, a man who had, until recently, known exactly who he was. He was the one who stayed calm, the one who could hold a scalpel steady while the world around him descended into chaos. He had chosen combat medicine because he believed in the logic of it—that the world, for all its brutality, was a place where a skilled hand and a clear mind could make a difference. That belief was shattered in a single, fragmented moment he can no longer fully piece together.

The event happened during a field hospital rotation near a forward operating base. A mass casualty event had come in—a firefight that had turned into an ambush. Samuel remembers the roar of the rotor blades, the shouting, the smell of blood and diesel. He remembers working on a young soldier, a tourniquet, a frantic call for more pressure. Then, a deafening explosion that collapsed the tent wall. He remembers nothing after that for what must have been minutes, only waking on his back, ears ringing, the silence around him suddenly the loudest thing he had ever experienced. He had a broken rib, a collapsed lung, and a memory that would no longer obey him.

The months that followed were a fog of disconnected images. He would be walking down a hospital corridor and suddenly see a flash of a face, a gloved hand, a puddle of crimson on a white floor. The pieces were there, but they did not fit. He could not sequence them. He could not tell you what had happened in the seconds between the blast and the waking. The harder he tried to push through the gaps, the more his mind seemed to slam a door shut, leaving him dizzy and gasping for air. He learned to stop trying. He began to push the memory away before it could fully form, a reflex that felt like survival but left him feeling hollow, as if the story of his own life had been ripped out of a book.

He returned to work, but the hospital was no longer a place of logic. Every shift became a minefield. A patient's sudden, violent struggle against sedation would send a shock through his chest, his hands trembling as he reached for a syringe. The worst trigger, however, was the breathlessness. A lingering effect of his lung injury meant that even climbing a flight of stairs could leave him winded. And that feeling—the tightness, the inability to get air in—would instantly transport him back to the moment he woke under the collapsed tent, convinced he was suffocating. He would have to excuse himself to a supply closet, gripping the shelves until his knuckles went white, certain he was about to die. He became hypervigilant to the air in his own lungs, monitoring every inhale and exhale with a dread he could not explain.

The silence, too, became an enemy. The sudden hush that falls over an emergency room after a code is called, the quiet of a break room between shifts—these moments felt more dangerous than any chaos. In silence, the fragmented pieces of memory would press in from the edges of his mind. He began to fill every quiet moment with noise, wearing earbuds on his commute, leaving the television on all night. Sleep, when it came, was shallow and interrupted.

What frightened Samuel most was not the memories themselves, but what they had done to him. He no longer recognized the man in the mirror. The confident doctor who had once thrived under pressure was gone, replaced by someone who jumped at a dropped bedpan and scanned every room for exits. His belief that hard work and skill could impose order on the world had been replaced by a creeping certainty that violence could erupt anywhere, at any time, and that he was helpless to stop it. He had to be on guard, he told himself, because no one else would be. But the guard was exhausting. It made him irritable with colleagues, distant from friends. He stopped returning calls from his family back in Nigeria, ashamed that he could not explain to them why he felt like a stranger in his own skin.

He finally sought help after a shift where a patient coded and he froze. Not for a second—for a full ten seconds, while a nurse had to shout his name twice. The look on her face, a mixture of fear and pity, was the final piece. He came to the clinic because he was afraid of what would happen if he did not, but also because, deep down, he hoped that somewhere in the gaps of his memory, there might still be a version of himself he could find again.
